sections.title: Foundations (Stages 1–2)
sections.description: First science ideas about living things, materials, forces and light from Stages 1 and 2.

questions.question: Which of these animals is a vertebrate — an animal with a backbone?
questions.options: a butterfly | a worm | a snail | a fish
questions.explanation: A fish has a backbone inside its body, so it is a vertebrate. Butterflies, snails and worms have no backbone at all.

questions.question: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, which living thing is the producer?
questions.options: the rabbit | the soil | the fox | the grass
questions.explanation: A producer makes its own food using sunlight. The grass does that, so every food chain like this one starts with a plant.

questions.question: A polar bear has thick fur that keeps it warm in the icy Arctic. What do we call a body feature like this that helps an animal survive in its habitat?
questions.options: an adaptation | a habit | a shadow | a skeleton
questions.explanation: A special feature that helps an animal live in its habitat is called an adaptation — like thick fur for the cold or a hump for the desert.

questions.question: A hedgehog is covered in sharp spines. What do the spines mostly help it to do?
questions.options: breathe underwater | make its own food | protect itself from predators | see in the dark
questions.explanation: When danger comes, a hedgehog rolls into a spiky ball. The sharp spines make it very hard for a predator to eat it.

questions.question: Wind can be used to make electricity, and the wind never gets used up. What do we call an energy source like this?
questions.options: non-renewable | renewable | electrical | invisible
questions.explanation: A renewable energy source, like wind or sunlight, will not run out — nature keeps supplying it. Coal and oil are non-renewable because one day they will be gone.

questions.question: Where does almost all the energy used by living things on Earth come from in the first place?
questions.options: the Sun | the Moon | the wind | the soil
questions.explanation: The Sun sends light energy to Earth. Plants use it to make food, animals eat the plants, and so the Sun’s energy passes along to every living thing.

questions.question: Why does your body need food every day?
questions.options: Food helps you see in the dark | Food stops your hair from growing | Food gives your body energy to move and grow | Food makes your bones heavier on purpose
questions.correctAnswer: Food gives your body energy to move and grow
questions.explanation: Food is your body’s fuel. It gives you the energy you need to run, play, think and grow.

questions.question: A puddle slowly disappears on a warm, sunny day. What is this change called?
questions.options: melting | evaporation | condensation | freezing
questions.explanation: The Sun warms the water and it turns into an invisible gas called water vapour, which rises into the air. That change from liquid to gas is evaporation.

questions.question: Which of these keeps its own shape without needing a container?
questions.options: steam | a wooden block | orange juice | the air in a balloon
questions.explanation: Solids like a wooden block keep their own shape. Liquids such as juice take the shape of their container, and gases like steam and air spread out to fill any space.

questions.question: Tiny water drops appear on the outside of a cold glass of juice. Where do the drops come from?
questions.options: The drops fall from the ceiling | The juice slowly leaks through the glass | The glass melts a little in the warm room | Water vapour in the air cools on the glass and turns into liquid
questions.correctAnswer: Water vapour in the air cools on the glass and turns into liquid
questions.explanation: The air always holds invisible water vapour. When it touches the cold glass it cools down and turns back into liquid drops — that change is called condensation.

questions.question: Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
questions.options: the clouds | the core | the mantle | the crust
questions.explanation: We live on the crust — the Earth’s thin, solid outer layer. The mantle and the core lie deep below it, far too hot to visit.

questions.question: What flows out of a volcano when it erupts?
questions.options: hot melted rock called lava | ice and snow | leaves and soil | cold sea water
questions.explanation: Deep underground the rock is so hot it melts. When a volcano erupts, that melted rock pours out at the top — above the ground we call it lava.

questions.question: What do we call the remains or print of an ancient living thing kept safe inside rock for millions of years?
questions.options: a magnet | a fossil | a pebble | a crystal
questions.explanation: A fossil is what is left of a plant or animal from long ago, preserved in rock. Fossils help scientists learn about life on Earth millions of years ago.

questions.question: A spoon does not make its own light. Why can you still see it?
questions.options: Your eyes send out light beams | The spoon makes a tiny bit of light | The spoon is warmer than the room | Light bounces off the spoon into your eyes
questions.correctAnswer: Light bounces off the spoon into your eyes
questions.explanation: We see things that make no light of their own because light from a source, like the Sun or a lamp, bounces off them and travels into our eyes.

questions.question: What must an object do to make a shadow?
questions.options: let all the light through | reflect all the light | block the light | make its own light
questions.explanation: A shadow is the dark space where light cannot reach. It forms when an object stands in the way and blocks the light.

questions.question: On a sunny day, when is your shadow the shortest?
questions.options: early in the morning | just after sunrise | late in the evening | around midday, when the Sun is highest
questions.correctAnswer: around midday, when the Sun is highest
questions.explanation: When the Sun is high overhead at midday, the light shines almost straight down, so your shadow shrinks. In the morning and evening the Sun is low and shadows stretch long.

questions.question: When will the bulb in a simple circuit light up?
questions.options: when there is a gap in the circuit | when the circuit makes a complete loop with no gaps | when the wires are very long | when the battery is taken out
questions.correctAnswer: when the circuit makes a complete loop with no gaps
questions.explanation: Electricity can only flow around a complete loop. If there is any gap in the circuit, the current stops and the bulb stays dark.

questions.question: What happens when you open the switch in a working circuit?
questions.options: The bulb shines more brightly | The wires turn into magnets | The battery charges itself up | It makes a gap, so the current stops and the bulb goes out
questions.correctAnswer: It makes a gap, so the current stops and the bulb goes out
questions.explanation: Opening a switch breaks the loop. The electricity cannot cross the gap, so the current stops flowing and the bulb goes out.

questions.question: Which of these is the safe choice around electricity?
questions.options: poking a metal fork into a socket | touching a fallen power line to move it | using a plugged-in hairdryer near a full bath | keeping water away from plugs and sockets
questions.correctAnswer: keeping water away from plugs and sockets
questions.explanation: Water lets electricity pass through it — and through you. Keeping water well away from plugs and sockets keeps you safe; the other three choices are very dangerous.

questions.question: Which of these shows that something is alive?
questions.options: It can be picked up | It grows and needs food | It is shiny | It is made of plastic
questions.explanation: Living things grow, feed, move, breathe and make new living things. Being shiny or easy to pick up tells us nothing about being alive.

questions.question: You stir sugar into warm water until you cannot see it any more. What has happened to the sugar?
questions.options: It has dissolved in the water | It has disappeared for ever | It has frozen solid | It has turned into water
questions.correctAnswer: It has dissolved in the water
questions.explanation: The sugar breaks into pieces too tiny to see and spreads through the water — it has dissolved. It is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet.

questions.question: Sara is testing which paper towel soaks up the most water. To make her test fair, what should she keep the same each time?
questions.options: the type of paper towel she tests | the amount of water she pours on each towel | the result she writes down | nothing — everything should change
questions.correctAnswer: the amount of water she pours on each towel
questions.explanation: In a fair test you change only the one thing you are testing — the towel — and keep everything else the same, like the amount of water. Then you know it was the towel that made the difference.

questions.question: Which of these makes its own light?
questions.options: a white wall | the Moon | the Sun | a mirror
questions.explanation: The Sun is a light source — it makes its own light. The Moon, a mirror and a white wall only bounce back light that comes from somewhere else.

questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around your whole body?
questions.options: the heart | the brain | the stomach | the lungs
questions.explanation: Your heart is a strong muscle that beats all day and night, pumping blood to every part of your body.

questions.question: Which of these objects will a magnet attract?
questions.options: a rubber band | a wooden pencil | a plastic ruler | a steel paper clip
questions.explanation: Magnets attract objects made of certain metals, like steel and iron. Plastic, wood and rubber are not magnetic, so the magnet leaves them alone.

questions.question: Why do we have day and night?
questions.options: The Earth spins around once each day | The Sun switches off every evening | The Moon covers the Sun at night | Clouds hide the Sun until morning
questions.correctAnswer: The Earth spins around once each day
questions.explanation: The Earth is always spinning. The side facing the Sun has daytime, and the side facing away has night — and one full spin takes about 24 hours.

questions.question: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.options: a stone | a chair | a bird | a toy car
questions.explanation: A bird grows, eats, breathes and has chicks — so it is alive. Stones, chairs and toy cars do none of those things.

questions.question: Which material is best for making a window you can see through?
questions.options: glass | wool | metal | wood
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent — light passes straight through it, so you can see out. Wood, metal and wool block the light.

questions.question: You kick a ball and it rolls away across the grass. What kind of force did your foot use on the ball?
questions.options: no force at all | a pull | a squeeze | a push
questions.explanation: Your foot pushed the ball away from you — a kick is a push. A pull would bring the ball closer instead.

questions.question: What do plants need so they can grow well?
questions.options: sweets and toys | light and water | darkness and dust | loud noise and smoke
questions.explanation: Plants grow well with light, water and air. Without light and water, a plant droops, turns pale and stops growing.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: What Do Animals and Plants Need to Live?

questions.question: Your room is completely dark. Which of these would help you see?
questions.options: turning on a torch | listening very carefully | putting on a warm hat | closing your eyes tightly
questions.explanation: We need light to see. In a completely dark room there is no light for your eyes to use, so turning on a torch — a light source — lets you see again.

questions.question: When can you see the Sun in the sky?
questions.options: only in winter | in the daytime | never | at midnight
questions.explanation: The Sun lights up the sky in the daytime. At night our side of the Earth has turned away from the Sun, so we cannot see it.
